-- prelude

This is the contents of the post
I wrote on >>discourse.atmosphere.community|
https://discourse.atmosphere.community>>
to start a discussion about NeoDoc.


-- tldr

I believe content portability is critical 
for a successful decentralized system. 
After all, being able to move your content 
doesn't do any good if no one else can 
use it. You're implicitly locked-in even 
though it looks like you're in control.

A few years ago, I designed a plain-text 
content format to replace Markdown on 
>>my sites| https://links.alanwsmith.com/ >>
I'm offering it as a potential option for
making portable, human-readable content 
in the Atmosphere. 

You can learn more about it at
>>neodoc.style| https://neodoc.style/ >>


-- title

NeoDoc and The Atmosphere

Hey folks,

I've been on Bluesky for a bit. It's only 
recently that I learned enough about the 
Atmosphere to start getting what it's all 
about. I don't remember the last time I 
was this excited about new tech. 

I saw standard.site kicking around a couple 
weeks ago. I jumped on it^^1^^. It's the kind 
of stuff I dream about^^2^^. 

One thing the leaflet post^^3^^ I saw about 
on standard.site mentions is that standard.site 
isn't a content standard. The only post^^4^^ 
I've seen on a content standard for the 
Atmosphere has to do with a wordpress lexicon 
for publishing HTML. 

I submit that HTML could work as a standardized 
content format. It's a battle tested standard 
that renders natively in browsers without 
modification. However, there are a couple 
things that recommend against it.


-- numbered

1. It's not friendly to write by hand. 
Unless you're hard-core, it's not something 
most folks are into. Offering the ability
for folks to write in plain text would
require putting tools in place to 
transform into HTML before storage. 
The algorithms for those transformations
would have be be standardized themselves. 

2. It's tough to standardize HTML content types. 
Microformats^^5^^ were an attempt. They never 
took off. That's at least partially because they 
lock the data into the rendering layer. Sure, 
you can do all kinds of things with CSS, but 
you have to set up a parser if you want to use 
the data independently. 


-- p

Markdown is another option. It's easy to learn 
and already has huge market share in the 
developer community. It's great for blog posts, 
but kinda sucks for anything beyond that. I 
mean, you can always roll your own HTML, but 
then your back to its unwieldy nature and
parsing complexity. 

Markdown also lacks the ability to add 
metadata to content. For example, say you want
to apply a custom style to an ``H2`` element 
on a page. There's no mechanism to do that 
in native Markdown. You have to switch to 
inline HTML.


-- h2

Introducing NeoDoc

There are other content formats out there. I 
reviewed a bunch when I got fed up with Markdown 
and decided to switch to something else for 
>>my sites| https://links.alanwsmith.com/ >>.
None offered the combination of flexibility 
and ease of use I was after. So, I designed 
a new one. It's called NeoDoc and you're 
reading it right now^^6^^.

The format is designed to be as
simple as possible without sacrificing 
horsepower. It breaks down like this:


-- list/
-- class: example

- NeoDocs are based on sections. Each one
starts with two dashes and a name. For 
example, the ``-- list`` from a few 
lines up. 

- Sections can have attributes like the
``-- class: example`` on this list
section. 

- There's a pre-defined set of sections like:
``-- list``, ``-- checklist``, and
``-- numbered``. 

- You can also make arbitrary sections 
types. For example, you can make a 
``-- book-review`` section for your
book reviews. 

- There's inline formatting and shorthands 
for spans of text. For example, you can
use astrisks to wrap a span in HTML strong
tags like this:

  -- code/

  **Alfa Bravo Charlie**

  -- /code


- The inline spans can have attributes as
well. For example, here's a class attribute
for the same strong shorthand:

  -- code/

  **Alfa Bravo Charlie|class: title**

  -- /code

-- /list


That's pretty much it. 

The rest of it comes down to processing. 
Details on that and how the everything works 
are on >>the NeoDoc site| https://neodoc.style >>.


-- h2


The Offering

I started working on NeoDoc three years 
ago. It's currently embedded in my personal 
static site generator. It powers the 
>>three thousand or so pages I've posted there|
https://www.alanwsmith.com/neo-files/report >>.

The format feels like a natural fit for 
the Atmosphere. So, I'm extracting it to 
make it generally available. Once it's 
ready, I'll make it open source so anyone 
can use it. 


-- h2

Outro

I'm incredibly excited about the potential 
of the Atmosphere. I hope NeoDoc can become 
a part of it. Because, if I'm right, the 
ability to easily move the stuff we make 
to wherever we want will be key to practical 
decentralization. And, I think NeoDoc
can fit that bill.

If you've got questions or feedback, 
I'm all ears:

>>@al9000.com|
https://bsky.app/profile/al9000.com >>

-a




-- endnote

I'd love to see NeoDoc become an active
participant in the Atmosphere. However, it's 
way more important to me that content gets
standardized on __something__, regardless of 
what it is. 

There will always be a need for custom formats 
for specific applications. For everything else, 
if we can't move it, it fails the promise 
and potential of decentralization. 


-- endnote/

The reference NeoDoc app (when it's extracted 
from my static site generator) performs
three functions:

  -- numbered/

  1. Takes a NeoDoc formatted input and 
  transforms it into a JSON formatted AST. 

  2. Transforms a NeoDoc AST into HTML 
  based on a standardized set of default 
  templates. 

  3. Accepts optional templates that override
  the defaults when generating output. 

  -- /numbered

More details on how all that works will
be in the docs. 

-- /endnote
